summary: Methodology for FiveThirtyEight's House, Senate and governor models from 2018, with 2020 and 2022 updates: the direct predecessor of FLIPR. It covers the Lite, Classic and Deluxe layers with their historical accuracy, poll inclusion and partisan-poll handling (sponsor-defined, lower weight, about 4-point bias prior), likely-voter, timeline and house-effect adjustments, CANTOR k-nearest-neighbor imputation with a selection-bias correction, the ranked list of fundamentals for incumbent races, Senate and governor differences, the 2022 changes (5x in-state money, a simple-plus-fancy fundamentals blend, more correlated errors, less sample-size weight), the expert-rating margin table, and four error types including incumbency-correlated error.

findings.statement: Version history: House model launched Aug. 16, 2018; top-two primaries and Pennsylvania redistricting handling added Aug. 20, 2018; race pages Aug. 26; Senate Sept. 12, 2018; governors Oct. 17, 2018; 2020 update Sept. 18, 2020 with a Senate-only forecast; 2022 update June 30, 2022. House and Senate forecasts are generated by the same program, with House data informing Senate and vice versa, while House and Senate data inform governors but not the reverse.
findings.evidence_quote: In fact, they’re literally generated by the same program, with data from House races informing the Senate forecasts and vice versa.

findings.statement: In 2022 the model began multiplying funds raised from within a candidate's state by 5 when assessing fundraising edge, because a dollar from in-state was found to be about five times as predictive as an out-of-state dollar.
findings.rationale: Empirically about five times as valuable in predicting outcomes.
findings.evidence_quote: We found that a dollar received from within a candidate’s state is about five times as valuable as a dollar received outside of it

findings.statement: In 2022 the model began blending its complex fundamentals formula with a simple alternative of partisan lean plus generic ballot. Tested on 2018 and 2020, the complex version slightly outperformed the simple one, but a blend beat either alone, so partisanship and the generic ballot gained influence relative to other fundamentals.
findings.evidence_quote: a blend of the complicated and simple formulas does better than either one taken alone.

findings.statement: In 2022 FiveThirtyEight increased the assumed correlation of race-by-race errors in congressional races, because polling errors were becoming more correlated even though correlation remains considerably lower than across states in presidential races. It also reduced the emphasis on sample size in poll weighting, consistent with a pollster-ratings change, and removed 2020 COVID-specific tweaks.
findings.evidence_quote: Therefore, we’ve increased the degree to which race-by-race errors are assumed to be correlated in the model.

findings.statement: 2020 congressional changes: fundamentals formulas adjusted so higher partisanship makes partisan lean more predictive and candidate quality less; house effects computed mostly from polls in the same state or district; Election Day error raised 20 percent for COVID and mail voting; CANTOR similarity including expected mail-vote share; Cost of Voting Index; Deluxe became the interactive default.
findings.evidence_quote: higher partisanship is associated with the partisan lean of a state or district being more predictive of election outcomes, while it makes candidate quality factors (such as the candidate’s level of experience) less predictive.

findings.statement: About three-quarters of the uncertainty in the House and Senate forecasts comes from local, race-by-race factors, unlike the presidential model where outcomes are extremely correlated across states. Governor races are even more localized, with partisanship a much weaker factor.

quantities.name: share of uncertainty from local factors

findings.evidence_quote: Nonetheless, about three-quarters of the uncertainty in the House and Senate forecasts comes from local, race-by-race factors.

findings.statement: Share of House races called correctly, 1998-2016 training data, 100 days out and on Election Day: Lite 94.2 and 96.2 percent; fundamentals alone 95.4 and 95.7; Classic 95.4 and 96.7; expert ratings alone 94.8 and 96.6; Deluxe 95.7 and 96.9. In training, Classic miscalled 3.3 percent of House races versus 3.8 for Lite.
findings.evidence_quote: In the training data, Classic miscalled 3.3 percent of House races, compared with 3.8 percent for Lite.

findings.statement: In 2018 FiveThirtyEight considered Classic its preferred version despite Deluxe being slightly more accurate, because borrowing others' forecasts felt like cheating; from 2020 Deluxe became the default display.
findings.rationale: Part of the point is testing a rigorous algorithm against subjective forecasts.
findings.evidence_quote: Basically, because we think it’s kind of cheating to borrow other people’s forecasts and make them part of our own.

findings.statement: The midterm models use almost all polls, including partisan and campaign polls, which make up about half of House district polling. Polls are excluded for veracity concerns or known fakers, DIY hobbyist polls on platforms like Google Surveys, subsamples of multistate polls unless conditions are met, and MRP or other blended or smoothed outputs, because FiveThirtyEight wants to do the blending itself.

quantities.name: partisan share of House district polling

findings.evidence_quote: We want to do the blending and smoothing ourselves rather than inputting other people’s models into ours.

findings.statement: Poll weights are set algorithmically from sample size, recency and pollster rating, never case by case. The algorithm emphasizes diversity, insisting on an average from at least two or three distinct firms in a race even if some polls are less recent.
findings.evidence_quote: it will insist on constructing an average of polls from at least two or three distinct polling firms even if some of the polls are less recent.

findings.statement: The midterm likely-voter adjustment is dynamic: it starts with a prior that LV polls slightly help Republicans, smaller in midterms with a Republican president, and updates as pollsters publish paired LV/RV results. FLIPR later replaced this with a more neutral prior.
findings.evidence_quote: it starts with a prior that likely voter polls slightly help Republicans, but this prior is updated as pollsters publish polls that directly compare likely and registered voter results.

findings.statement: The congressional timeline adjustment shifts a race poll by roughly two-thirds of the subsequent generic ballot change in congressional races and about half in gubernatorial races, modulated by the state's or district's elasticity. It is much more conservative than the presidential model's timeline adjustment.
findings.evidence_quote: by roughly two-thirds that amount in congressional races and half that amount in gubernatorial races, depending on the elasticity score of the state or district

findings.statement: Polls are classified as partisan by sponsor, not by who conducts them: a candidate, party, campaign committee, or a PAC, super PAC or 501(c)(4/5/6) mostly active for one party. Partisan polls get lower weight and a house-effect prior of about 4 points toward the sponsor's side, overridden if the pollster's results match nonpartisan polls over time.
findings.rationale: Partisan-sponsored polls are historically less accurate.
findings.evidence_quote: the house effects adjustment starts out with a prior that assumes these polls are biased by about 4 percentage points toward their preferred candidate or party.

findings.statement: CANTOR uses a k-nearest neighbors algorithm on demographic, geographic and political factors to find similar districts and states; districts can be compared with states. Stage one guesses what polls would show from partisan lean and incumbency, e.g. Republican incumbents polling poorly where polled suggests vulnerability elsewhere. Stage two adjusts by similarity scores. Projections are corrected for selection bias, since unpolled districts tend to be less competitive. Governor races do not feed CANTOR for House and Senate, but House and Senate feed governors.
findings.evidence_quote: It uses a k-nearest neighbors algorithm to identify similar congressional districts and states based on a variety of demographic, geographic and political factors.

findings.statement: In competitive House races with incumbents, the fundamentals that best predicted results, in roughly declining order, were: (1) the incumbent's previous margin, adjusted for the national environment and the prior opponent; (2) the generic ballot; (3) fundraising share of individual contributions; (4) partisan lean; (5) congressional approval; (6) scandals involving either candidate; (7) the incumbent's roll-call party loyalty over the past three Congresses, with mavericks outperforming; (8) the challenger's elected experience. The analysis focused on competitive races.
findings.evidence_quote: In competitive House districts with incumbents, the following factors have historically best predicted election results, in roughly declining order of importance:

findings.statement: The 2018 FiveThirtyEight partisan lean formula gives 50 percent weight to the 2016 presidential election, 25 percent to 2012, and 25 percent to state legislative elections, the same structure Silver Bulletin used in 2026.
findings.evidence_quote: In our partisan lean formula, 50 percent of the weight is given to the 2016 presidential election, 25 percent to the 2012 presidential election and 25 percent to state legislative elections.

findings.statement: Senate fundamentals differ from House ones: the previous margin is less reliable because six years have passed; incumbency advantage is larger in smaller, more demographically distinct states; the model accounts for changes in state partisanship since the seat was last contested; and it uses a more advanced candidate-experience measure.
findings.evidence_quote: the Senate model uses more sophisticated data in calculating the effects of incumbency.

findings.statement: Gubernatorial fundamentals use the Senate factors except roll-call ideology, which is not used, and fundraising based on all contributions from the Campaign Finance Institute. The generic ballot is about two-thirds as predictive as for Congress and partisan lean about one-third as predictive: a state 12 points Democratic for Congress projects only about 4 points Democratic for governor.
findings.evidence_quote: A state that leans toward the Democrats by 12 points in a race for Congress would be predicted to do so by only about 4 points in a race for governor, for example.

findings.statement: Open-seat races use the non-incumbency factors (generic ballot, fundraising, partisan lean, scandals, experience, top-two primary results where applicable) plus the previous congressional result, which is much less reliable than with an incumbent. Previous results are not used in open governor races. In 2018, Pennsylvania redistricting was handled by population overlap, and California and Washington top-two primary results were used.
findings.evidence_quote: Previous election results aren’t used at all in gubernatorial races without incumbents.

findings.statement: Classic and Deluxe compare their current national environment to a prior based on congressional elections since 1946, accounting for historic midterm swings and presidential approval; the prior phases out completely by Election Day.
findings.evidence_quote: The prior is designed in such a way that it phases it out completely by Election Day.

findings.statement: Average margin of victory by expert rating in House races since 1998: Toss-up 0 points; Tilt 4; Lean 7; Likely 12; Solid or Safe 34. The rating database covers House and governor races since 1998 and Senate since 1990. Solid ratings barely move projections unless other factors suggest the race should be competitive.

Expert raters are excellent at micro conditions but lag on the macro environment; for example they shifted sharply toward Democrats in early 2018 while the generic ballot was steady. Deluxe therefore blends the experts' relative ordering of races with Classic's data-driven national estimate, so Deluxe and Classic usually agree on total seats while possibly disagreeing on individual races.
findings.evidence_quote: they tend to be lagging indicators of the macro political environment.

findings.statement: The midterm models account for four error types: (1) local error, larger with less polling, conflicting indicators, or high elasticity, such as New Hampshire versus the bifurcated South; (2) regional and demographic error simulated with CANTOR similarity; (3) incumbency-driven error, for instance polls systematically underestimating Republican incumbents; (4) a uniform national swing, smaller for governor races. Error shrinks as Election Day approaches.
findings.evidence_quote: Third, there can be error driven by incumbency status.

findings.statement: The midterm models project turnout in each race from the eligible population and past midterm and presidential turnout, with competitive races producing higher turnout. Turnout matters for translating the national popular vote into seats.
findings.evidence_quote: Projecting turnout is important in understanding the relationship between the national popular vote and the number of seats that each party might gain or lose.

findings.statement: FiveThirtyEight does not make ad hoc adjustments to individual race forecasts; everything is done strictly by algorithm.
findings.evidence_quote: I should emphasize that we do not make ad-hoc adjustments to the forecasts in individual races.

political_insights.insight: Incumbents who vote against their party more often outperform electorally, other factors equal.
political_insights.evidence: Roll-call loyalty over past three Congresses.

references.description: Campaign Finance Institute gubernatorial fundraising data

open_questions: CANTOR's specific demographic, geographic and political variables and the k used in k-nearest neighbors.
Size of the incumbency-correlated error component.
